title: Senate Crypto Vote Tests Trump's Financial Entanglements
summary:
The Senate is set to vote Tuesday on whether to move forward with legislation creating a new regulatory framework for cryptocurrency, a pivotal election-year test for the $2.3 trillion market. The vote comes just two months before the midterm elections, as the crypto industry has become a major political force and President Donald Trump has amassed significant crypto wealth while in office.

While some Democrats support the idea of a regulatory framework — a top priority for the industry — the party has been mostly united in opposition unless the bill includes strong ethics safeguards to prevent the president and his family from enriching themselves. "Let's make sure that we do not pass a crypto bill that will let Donald Trump continue to rake in billions of dollars in crypto profits while working families across this country struggle to deal with higher prices," said Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee.

As Democrats have vowed to block the bill, Trump has agreed to some concessions on ethics, including new restrictions on federal elected officials issuing digital assets like the presidential meme coins he and his wife Melania launched before he took office for his second term. On Sunday, Trump agreed to additional concessions, such as additional powers for state attorneys general that Democrats had sought. But those concessions do not appear to be enough for most Democrats.

A proposal by Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina had sought to require Trump to put his crypto holdings in a blind trust and divest when those holdings reach a certain value. The latest version of the bill "leaves a lot to be desired," Gallego said Monday evening. "If they think this is a final deal, this is not their call."

Republicans need Democratic support to win the 60 votes necessary to move forward in the 53-47 Senate. Trump's family has raked in big profits in the crypto sector since he was reelected, including the meme coin announced the day before Trump took office. Trump reported more than $500 million in revenue from World Liberty Financial sales of crypto products in his annual disclosure report. That is a significant share of the more than $1.4 billion the president reported from crypto businesses last year. Supporters say the legislation aims to give the industry more legal certainty and protect consumers by creating a broad set of guardrails. Opponents say it is a giveaway to the industry, which spent more than $130 million in 2024 congressional races.
why_it_matters: This vote tests whether Congress can write rules for a fast-growing industry at the same time that it is supposed to police the sitting president's own financial interests — a conflict-of-interest question that will outlast this one bill and shape how money and politics mix for years.

background_read: The U.S. Senate has 100 members, and most bills need 60 votes to move forward because of the filibuster — a rule that lets a minority block legislation unless three-fifths of senators agree to proceed, which forces deals across party lines in a closely divided chamber.

Cryptocurrency is digital money that runs on blockchain networks rather than through a central bank; in the United States it has been policed by a patchwork of agencies, which the industry says makes it hard to operate legally and which critics say leaves consumers exposed.

Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, has pushed for years for stricter rules on crypto and on possible conflicts of interest for public officials, while Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Thom Tillis of North Carolina represent a more cross-party approach.

Federal ethics law already requires presidents and other officials to disclose their finances, but it does not force them to sell assets — which is why proposals for a blind trust, where an official hands investments to a manager and does not know what is owned, keep coming up.

The crypto industry became a major political spender in the 2024 elections, when crypto-backed super PACs poured money into congressional races, making the sector one of the fastest-growing lobbying forces in Washington.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the crypto industry and its allies
perspectives.description: Supporters argue the bill would replace a confusing patchwork of regulators with clear national rules, giving companies the legal certainty they need to build and invest in the United States. They say the consumer guardrails in the legislation are a genuine improvement over the current situation, where investors have little protection.

Critics say the safeguards are far too weak while the president's family earns hundreds of millions from the very sector being regulated, calling the bill a giveaway to an industry that spent heavily to influence Congress. They argue the ethics provisions were watered down late in the process, and that the Gallego–Tillis blind-trust idea was the minimum needed.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral / analytical — how the Senate actually works
perspectives.description: With a 53-47 Senate, the 60-vote threshold means no crypto bill passes without Democratic support, so both parties are negotiating from a position of mutual dependence. The episode also shows how quickly a young industry can become a lobbying force, mirroring earlier battles over railroads, banks and the internet.

If the bill advances, courts and agencies will spend years defining how far the new rules and ethics limits reach; if it stalls, the industry will keep pushing and the midterms will become a referendum on it. Either way, questions about a president's business holdings are likely to follow Trump well past this vote.
